worlds.question: Why do nominally identical 3D-printed polymer tensile coupons show persistent strength differences?
worlds.target_hypothesis: Process-temperature variation explains most of the persistent tensile-strength difference.

modules.descriptor: Repeated baseline production and retest series
modules.evidence: Across six repeated baseline batches, tensile strength remains separated into two persistent clusters. The gap is stable across same-day retests.

modules.descriptor: Controlled variation of candidate process settings
modules.evidence: Small controlled changes in nozzle temperature shift mean strength modestly, but the observed shift explains only part of the full cluster gap.
Most low-strength coupons trace to two resin-storage histories and one printer-maintenance interval; temperature settings overlap substantially across high- and low-strength groups.
A temperature-only model leaves large structured residuals and does not reproduce several low-strength batches.

modules.descriptor: Targeted intervention on the leading candidate factor
modules.evidence: Holding resin handling and machine state fixed while changing temperature narrows but does not eliminate the strength difference.
Temperature sensitivity is strongest for one polymer lot and weak for the others, indicating a boundary-specific interaction.
Gauge repeatability is high and destructive-test calibration checks show measurement error is too small to explain the persistent gap.
The main residual pattern persists under alternate normalization, exclusion rules, and robust regression, although effect sizes vary.

worlds.question: Why do sites using the same nominal warehouse process show persistent completion-time differences?
worlds.target_hypothesis: Shift-handoff quality explains most of the persistent completion-time difference.

modules.descriptor: Repeated baseline site and shift series
modules.evidence: Across eight repeated weeks, completion-time differences remain stable by site and persist after excluding unusual demand spikes.

modules.descriptor: Controlled variation of candidate process settings
modules.evidence: Improving handoff checklist compliance reduces completion time modestly, but the shift is smaller than the full persistent site gap.
Slow periods cluster with staffing-mix changes and equipment congestion episodes; handoff scores overlap considerably between faster and slower sites.
A handoff-only model leaves large site-structured residuals and misses several slow periods with strong handoff scores.

modules.descriptor: Targeted intervention on the leading candidate factor
modules.evidence: A handoff-standardization intervention improves time at some sites but does not remove persistent between-site differences.
Handoff effects are largest on high-turnover evening shifts and small on stable daytime shifts, indicating effect modification.
Timestamp audits and duplicate logging checks show measurement error is small relative to the persistent completion-time gap.
The remaining site pattern persists under alternate workload adjustments, trimming rules, and robust models.
